implementation_notes: The base C++ realization: a command is a `std::function<void()>` (type-erased closure) or a `std::packaged_task<R()>` when the submitter needs the result, the repository is a `std::queue<...>` guarded by `std::mutex` and `std::condition_variable`, and the executor is a fixed set of worker threads that pop-and-run outside the lock; `std::future` from packaged_task gives the result, cancellation-by-policy and the per-command outcome that the history layer records. Undo and macros are application-level: store a serialisable command description plus an inverse alongside the closure, or keep a separate `std::function<void()>` undo stack. Still the right choice when no third-party runtime may be added.
pitfalls: Holding the mutex while executing the command serialises the pool and deadlocks on re-submission; dequeue under the lock, execute outside it.
Discarding the std::future of a std::packaged_task loses the exception it carries - the failure becomes silent.
A command capturing `this` or a reference outlives the object it refers to if it stays in the queue/history; prefer capturing values or shared ownership.
An unbounded std::queue with no backpressure policy turns overload into unbounded memory growth.

variants.name: Boost.Asio io_context as a ready-made executor
variants.implementation_notes: Boost.Asio already provides the processor's executor: `io_context::post()` enqueues a handler into io_context's own work queue and a thread or thread pool running `io_context::run()` drains it - commands are the posted handlers and scheduling policy becomes thread count plus `strand` serialisation. This removes the hand-written queue/mutex/condvar triple, and it is the pragmatic choice when the process is I/O-bound and Asio is already in the build; the command abstraction (typed commands, history, undo) is still application code, and only one participant (the executor) came from the library.
pitfalls: Without a work_guard, `io_context::run()` returns as soon as the queue empties and the pool stops draining commands.
Multiple threads calling run() execute handlers concurrently - wrap commands that must not interleave in a strand or raise max_concurrency to 1.
Long blocking work inside a posted handler stalls the event loop; hand it to a separate thread pool and post the completion back.
